title: Ordinary Jobs Footballers Had Before Turning Pro | WinFulltime
description: From sausage factories to beetroot bottling plants, these famous footballers worked ordinary jobs before turning professional and finding stardom.
keywords: footballers ordinary jobs, footballers who worked factory jobs, footballer day jobs, Chris Waddle job, Jamie Vardy factory, Rickie Lambert beetroot
h1: Ordinary Jobs Footballers Had Before Turning Pro
lead: Not every future star spends their teenage years in an academy. Many of the game's most famous names earned a wage in a sausage factory, a beetroot plant or a Ford assembly line before a football club ever signed them.
thumbCaption: Famous footballers who worked ordinary jobs before turning pro
share: Before the millions, there were factory shifts. The footballers who worked ordinary jobs before turning professional.
content:
The path to professional football is usually drawn as a straight line: a boy is spotted in a school game, joins an academy, and climbs every rung until a first-team debut. The reality has never been that tidy. Plenty of household names spent years doing work a football club would never advertise, stacking shelves, bottling vegetables or pressing car parts, before injury, luck or a late trial changed everything.

Why So Many Careers Start Off the Pitch

The modern academy system makes it easy to forget that, for most of football's history, players were signed in their late teens or early twenties straight from workplaces, not youth setups. Before the 1990s, a teenager who was released by a club had no structured route back in. He found a job, kept playing at amateur level, and prayed for a second chance.

That second chance came for an extraordinary number of the game's biggest names. Here are some of the most famous footballers who worked ordinary jobs before turning professional.

Chris Waddle — The Sausage Factory

Before he was running down the wing for Newcastle, Marseille and England, Chris Waddle worked at a sausage factory in his native County Durham. He was a butcher's apprentice before that, earning pennies while playing non-league football for Tow Law Town in the evenings. He was 21 before he finally got a professional contract, proving that the 'too old to make it' story is almost always a myth.

Les Ferdinand — The Ford Assembly Line

For nine years Les Ferdinand combined a full-time job at the Ford plant in Dagenham with his football career. He was famously a trade union shop steward, only turning fully professional when Queens Park Rangers signed him at 22. By the time he retired he had scored more than 150 Premier League goals and won 17 England caps — not bad for a player who reported to the assembly line every morning.

Peter Schmeichel — From Cleaner to World Class

Few goalkeepers have dominated a generation like Peter Schmeichel, yet his route was anything but privileged. The Danish legend worked in a textile factory, took shifts as a cleaner and laid flooring before making it as a professional. He was also a handball player as a young man, which helps explain the extraordinary 'star jump' reflex saves that became his trademark at Manchester United.

Rickie Lambert — The Beetroot Plant

Rickie Lambert did not just have an ordinary job, he had one of the most absurd ones in football history. Released by Liverpool and Blackpool as a teenager, he signed for Stockport County and was soon loaned to Macclesfield Town. With his career stalling he took a job in a beetroot bottling plant in Liverpool to make ends meet, reportedly while still a free agent. Years later he was scoring on his England debut, at 32, as the unlikely hero of a fairytale career.

Jamie Vardy — Making Medical Splints

When Leicester City were preparing for their title charge, few knew their future talisman Jamie Vardy had spent his early twenties as a technician making medical splints in a factory in Sheffield. Playing part-time for Stocksbridge Park Steels, he juggled factory shifts with Saturday football until Fleetwood Town signed him — and within two years he was a Premier League record signing and an FA Cup and Premier League winner.

Mickey Quinn — The Taxi Driver Striker

Mickey Quinn, who scored 102 Premier League goals for Newcastle, Everton and Coventry, kept a taxi-driving licence for years. The Liverpudlian striker's day job was as legendary as his finishing; he worked as a cabbie during the early part of his career at Wigan and Bradford City, and the story still follows him around to this day.

Ian Wright — The Plasterer

Ian Wright was 22 and still playing Sunday league football while working as a plasterer and builder when Crystal Palace took a chance on him. The rest is Arsenal legend: 185 goals for the Gunners and a Ballon d'Or-nominated peak. Wright has often said the years of manual labour gave him the hunger and finishing power that defined his career.

The Lesson of the Day Jobs

There is a pattern running through all of these stories. None of these players was an overnight prodigy handed everything at age nine. They were late developers, released or overlooked, who kept playing because they loved it and kept working because they had to.

The takeaway: A late start is not a barrier to greatness. What matters is whether the player is still learning, still hungry and still improving when the second chance finally arrives.

That is why talent scouts still watch non-league and lower-division football so closely. The next Vardy or Lambert could be out there now, finishing a factory shift before a Tuesday night cup tie.

title: Footballers Who Almost Chose Another Sport | WinFulltime
description: Petr Cech nearly chose ice hockey, Zlatan almost took up taekwondo, and Gareth Bale is a scratch golfer. Meet the football stars who nearly picked another sport.
keywords: footballers another sport, Petr Cech ice hockey, Zlatan taekwondo, Gareth Bale golf, footballers who almost played other sports, cross-sport footballers
h1: Footballers Who Almost Chose Another Sport
lead: A handful of the game's greatest players were once equally good at something else entirely — an ice hockey goal, a taekwondo black belt, a scratch golf handicap. Here is what football very nearly lost.
thumbCaption: Famous footballers who almost chose another sport
share: Ice hockey, taekwondo, golf, tennis — the other sports these football legends almost chose instead.
content:
Every footballer has a story about how they started. Most involve a garden, a brother, a school team. But a select few have a different tale to tell: they were genuinely good at another sport first, sometimes better, and football only won because of a twist of fate, a body that grew the wrong way, or a decision made by a parent.

Petr Cech — The Ice Hockey Goalkeeper

Petr Cech is the most famous example of a player who nearly ended up in a different sport. The Czech grew up wanting to be an ice hockey goaltender and played competitively as a child. He only abandoned hockey at around age ten, when his legs outgrew his equipment, and turned to football instead. The positional instincts stayed with him: after retiring from football he actually returned to hockey as a player, turning out for Guildford Phoenix in 2019, and later played for Oxford City Stars. The man simply never lost the goalie's mentality.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic — Taekwondo Black Belt

Before he was the most theatrical striker of his generation, Zlatan Ibrahimovic trained in taekwondo at a club in Malmö as a young boy. He was good enough to hold an honorary black belt, and his famous bicycle kicks and impossible acrobatics are routinely credited, in part, to the footwork and flexibility he learned on the mats. He gave up the discipline for football, but the martial arts movement stayed in his game for twenty years.

Gareth Bale — Scratch Golfer

After retiring from football, Gareth Bale set about a second sporting career in golf, and there was nothing casual about it. The former Real Madrid and Wales winger carries a handicap close to scratch — the level of a very serious amateur — and has played in celebrity pro-am events at Pebble Beach alongside professionals. His famous 'Wales. Golf. Madrid. In that order' celebration was a joke that turned out to be half true.

Karim Benzema — The Tennis Prospect

Before France's record-breaker committed fully to football, Karim Benzema was a promising young tennis player. Growing up in Lyon, he played the sport seriously, and friends and coaches from the period remember a talented junior who could have pursued the game further. He chose football, and the world is glad he did, but the hand-eye coordination he built on the tennis court never hurt his first touch.

Peter Schmeichel — The Handball Athlete

Long before his Manchester United heroics, Peter Schmeichel was a gifted handball player, a sport with far more prestige in Denmark than football had at the time. He was a junior athlete before his growth spurt pushed him toward the goal, and his extraordinary reflexes and the famous 'star jump' — arms and legs spread wide to make himself impossible to beat — came straight from handball goalkeeping.

Why Cross-Sport Athletes Thrive

What connects Cech, Zlatan, Bale, Benzema and Schmeichel is more than a trivia answer. Athletes who nearly chose another sport tend to bring a transferable skill set with them:

  • Hand-eye coordination — from tennis, golf and hockey, improving striking and reflexes.
  • Body control — from martial arts and gymnastics, enabling acrobatic finishing.
  • Explosiveness — from sprinting and basketball, adding pace and leaping power.
  • Composure — from individual sports, where you only have yourself to rely on.
The pattern: Very few world-class footballers were ever one-sport athletes. The ones who were nearly lost to another sport often become the most adaptable players of their generation.

The Ones Who Did Both

Some players did not have to choose at all. Cech returned to ice hockey after retirement, Bale keeps playing elite amateur golf, and former sprint champion Usain Bolt famously attempted a football trial after retiring from the track — proof that for elite athletes, the sporting instinct never fully switches off.

So the next time you watch a striker produce an impossible finish, wonder what they might have been doing instead. The answer, somewhere, is probably a hockey rink, a tennis court or a golf course.

h1: The Footballers With the Most Club Appearances
lead: Fifty years of football produces a lot of games. The players who have taken the pitch the most times form a who's who of durability, from a Brazilian goalkeeper who now holds the world record to the one-club legends of European football.
thumbCaption: Ranking the footballers with the most club appearances
share: Who has played the most football matches ever? The all-time appearance record now belongs to a Brazilian goalkeeper called Fábio.
content:
Goals win headlines, but appearances are the true currency of longevity. To reach a thousand professional games a player must stay fit, stay selected and stay relevant for two decades, surviving every new signing the club makes in his position. That is why the all-time appearance record is one of the most respected numbers in the game.

The New All-Time Record: Fábio

In October 2025, Brazilian goalkeeper Fábio passed a milestone that had stood for decades. Fábio, who has spent his entire career in Brazil with Cruzeiro and then Fluminense, reached 1,433 official matches, overtaking the previous all-time record set by England legend Peter Shilton. At 44 years old, he is still playing and still extending the record with every match.

Shilton's total of 1,387 official career matches had been considered unbreakable, because it combined a three-decade career with an extraordinary run of domestic cup and league appearances. Fábio's longevity — goalkeeper, remarkably durable, consistently first choice — has now written him into the record books.

Rogerio Ceni: The Single-Club Record

While Fábio owns the overall record, the most appearances for a single club belongs to another Brazilian goalkeeper. Rogerio Ceni made more than 1,200 official appearances for São Paulo between 1990 and 2015 — the most any player has ever played for one team. He also scored 128 career goals, making him the highest-scoring goalkeeper in football history, a combination of records that will likely never be repeated.

The All-Time Top Club Appearance Makers

Different sources count official matches slightly differently — some include friendly internationals and cup replays, others do not. Using the widely cited official-match figures, the all-time list looks like this:

PlayerClub(s)Official matches
FábioCruzeiro, Fluminense1,433
Peter ShiltonLeicester, Stoke, Nottm Forest, Southampton, Derby, etc.1,387
Rogerio CeniSão Paulo1,200+
Roberto CarlosPalmeiras, Inter, Real Madrid, Fenerbahce1,100+
Ryan GiggsManchester United963
Paolo MaldiniAC Milan902
Javier ZanettiInter Milan858
Francesco TottiRoma786
Iker CasillasReal Madrid, Porto880+
Frank LampardWest Ham, Chelsea, Man City870+

Figures in this table follow official competitive matches only and are rounded where sources differ by a handful of games. What matters is the pattern: the all-time list is dominated by goalkeepers, defenders and central midfielders — positions where a top player can still perform into their late thirties.

Why Goalkeepers Dominate the Record

Look at the two records above and one fact stands out: the all-time appearance leader and the single-club appearance leader are both goalkeepers. The reasons are obvious.

  • Goalkeepers suffer far fewer muscle injuries and almost no joint wear from sprinting.
  • They do not get dropped for form as often as outfield players.
  • A goalkeeper's prime runs from 25 to 35, and many play on far beyond that.
Fun fact: Fábio is 44 and still first choice. His closest rival, Shilton, played his final professional match at 47. The appearance record may yet stand for another half century.

Can Anyone Ever Catch Fábio?

To break 1,433 appearances, a player starting at 18 would need to average more than 50 matches a season for 27 years. Modern football's heavier workload makes that harder, not easier. The chances are that the next record-holder is currently a goalkeeper, in his teens, who nobody has heard of yet.

Appearances are football's quietest record, and its hardest to break. For more on the records that may never fall, see our guide to unbreakable football records.

title: The Most Loyal One-Club Footballers in History | WinFulltime
description: Totti, Maldini, Giggs and Puyol spent entire careers at one club. Meet the one-club footballers who defined loyalty — and why they are vanishing.
keywords: one club footballers, one club men, Francesco Totti Roma, Paolo Maldini AC Milan, Ryan Giggs Manchester United, player loyalty football, one club legends
h1: The Most Loyal One-Club Footballers in History
lead: Some players are a club. They arrive as schoolboys and leave only on the final day of their career, having turned down every offer the world could make. These are the greatest one-club men in football history.
thumbCaption: The greatest one-club footballers in history
share: Francesco Totti, Paolo Maldini, Ryan Giggs — the one-club legends who turned down the world.
content:
Modern football runs on transfers. Squads are rebuilt every summer, agents shop their clients around, and a player staying at one club for a decade is increasingly treated as a rarity. But for a golden generation of professionals, one club was enough. Their loyalty built dynasties, retired shirt numbers and created the kind of bond between player and supporter that money cannot buy.

What Makes a One-Club Man

A genuine one-club footballer plays his entire senior career for a single team. That usually means joining as a youth player or teenager and finishing as a veteran, decade after decade, at the same stadium. Every year they stay, they are implicitly turning down contracts elsewhere — often for more money, sometimes for a better shot at trophies.

Francesco Totti — Roma, 1993 to 2017

No one embodies the one-club ideal like Francesco Totti. The Roman spent his entire career at his hometown club, making 786 appearances and scoring 307 goals for Roma between 1993 and 2017. He turned down Real Madrid and Manchester United at his peak, won the 2001 Serie A title and the 2006 World Cup with Italy, and is treated as royalty in the Italian capital to this day.

Paolo Maldini — AC Milan, 1985 to 2009

Paolo Maldini played 902 matches for AC Milan across 24 seasons, winning five European Cups and seven Serie A titles. He never played a competitive minute for any other club, and his family name is now part of Milan's identity. His 902 appearances stand as one of the great durability records in European football.

Ryan Giggs — Manchester United, 1991 to 2014

Ryan Giggs made 963 appearances for Manchester United over a 24-year career, winning 13 Premier League titles, two Champions League crowns and the FA Cup four times. He debuted as a 17-year-old winger and retired as a veteran, one-club loyalty wrapped around the most successful era in the club's history.

Carles Puyol and the Barcelona Core

Carles Puyol spent his whole career at Barcelona, making 593 appearances and lifting everything the club could win between 1999 and 2014. He was the defensive heartbeat of the golden era that included Xavi, Iniesta and Messi — himself a one-club man for Barcelona for over 20 years, even if his final move to Inter Miami closed the door on a purely one-club career.

The English One-Club Legends

England has produced its own pantheon of one-club men:

PlayerClubYearsAppearances
Tony AdamsArsenal1983–2002672
Paul ScholesManchester United1994–2013718
Gary NevilleManchester United1992–2011602
Jamie CarragherLiverpool1996–2013737

Each of these players was repeatedly linked with moves abroad or to rivals and each stayed, usually at some financial cost to themselves.

Why One-Club Men Are Disappearing

The modern game makes the one-club career harder than ever. There are three structural reasons:

  • Contract economics — the biggest wages are only available at the richest clubs, so loyalty often means earning less.
  • Transfer culture — agents and release clauses turn every strong season into a potential move.
  • Manager turnover — a player who outlasts three managers at one club is rare, because each manager rebuilds.
Reality check: A one-club career today almost requires the player to be both elite and deeply rooted in the city. That combination is why the next Totti or Maldini may already be the last of their kind.

description: Lionel Messi leads the all-time trophy count with 46 senior honours. See the full ranking of the most decorated footballers, from Dani Alves to Hossam Hassan.

h1: The Most Decorated Footballers of All Time
lead: Medals are the true measure of a career. From Lionel Messi's record haul to the African and European legends chasing him, here are the most decorated footballers in history.
thumbCaption: Ranking the most decorated footballers of all time
share: Messi leads the all-time trophy ranking with 46 titles. The most decorated footballers in history, ranked.
content:
Individual awards tell one story. Trophies tell another. Winning a league title takes a full season of consistency; winning a cup takes knockout nerves; winning a World Cup takes a four-year peak. The players who stacked up all of them, season after season, are the most decorated footballers in history — and the list is a who's who of the game's great dynasties.

Messi Extends the Record

As of the 2026 summer, Lionel Messi sits alone at the top of the all-time list with 46 senior career trophies. That total counts every major competition he won with Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, plus the 2022 World Cup and Copa America titles with Argentina. It is the largest haul any footballer has ever collected.

Counting caveat: Trophy counts depend on what is included. Some rankings count only 'senior' honours, others add youth and underage titles, which is why you will see Messi quoted anywhere from 44 to 48. The universally accepted senior figure is 46.

The All-Time Trophy Ranking

PlayerCountrySenior trophies
Lionel MessiArgentina46
Dani AlvesBrazil43
Hossam HassanEgypt41
Hossam AshourEgypt39
Andres IniestaSpain37
MaxwellBrazil37
Gerard PiqueSpain37
Cristiano RonaldoPortugal35
Ryan GiggsWales34

Counts follow the widely cited senior-trophy totals. Note how the list splits into two families: the Barcelona golden generation (Messi, Alves, Iniesta, Pique, Maxwell) and the Egyptian dominance of Hossam Hassan and Hossam Ashour, whose hauls were built on Al Ahly's record run of African titles.

How the Barcelona Core Stacked Them Up

Between 2008 and 2015, Barcelona won everything available, and the same players collected medals for all of it. Dani Alves won 43 trophies across Brazil, Spain and Italy, spending nine trophy-laden years at Barcelona. Andres Iniesta, Gerard Pique and Lionel Messi each won ten La Liga titles, four Champions Leagues and countless cups, and then added the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2008 and 2012 with Spain.

The African Giants: Hossam Hassan and Hossam Ashour

It is easy to forget that the all-time list is not purely European. Hossam Hassan, the Egyptian striker, won 41 trophies in a 30-year career spanning Al Ahly, Zamalek and the Egyptian national team. His countryman Hossam Ashour collected 39, almost all of them with Al Ahly, whose dominance of the CAF Champions League produced a medal haul no European defender could match.

Why the Record May Never Move Again

To pass Messi, a player born in the 2020s would need to win roughly four trophies a year for twelve years straight — and that is before they count. More realistically, the modern Champions League format and expanded domestic calendars make deep trophy hauls slightly harder, and the dominance of one or two clubs means medals are concentrated among fewer players.

The most decorated footballer in history is, for now, comfortably Lionel Messi. For the full story of Egypt's decorated captain, see our dedicated profile of Hossam Ashour.

h1: Footballers Who Won Every Major Trophy
lead: Most great players never win a World Cup. A tiny handful win every trophy the sport offers. These are the footballers who completed the grand slam — and the decade of dominance that made it possible.
thumbCaption: The footballers who won every major trophy
share: Xavi, Iniesta, Busquets and Messi won every trophy football offers. How the grand slam was completed.
content:
There is a phrase used loosely in football: 'he has won everything.' In almost every case, it is not true. Winning everything means collecting every trophy a player can realistically enter — and for the very best, that list ends with the World Cup, the hardest competition in the sport to win. It takes an entire career of elite peak timing, plus the luck of a perfect international cycle.

What 'Everything' Actually Means

For a European club footballer, the grand slam looks like this:

  • Domestic league title
  • Domestic cup
  • UEFA Champions League
  • UEFA Super Cup and FIFA Club World Cup
  • A senior international trophy — and ultimately the World Cup

Winning the first four is possible for a superstar at a dominant club. Winning the international half requires a national team to align with your peak years — something no player controls.

The Barcelona Golden Generation

The cleanest grand slams in modern history were completed by the core of Barcelona's great side. Xavi, Andres Iniesta, Sergio Busquets and Gerard Pique each won:

TrophyWhere they won it
La LigaBarcelona (multiple titles)
Copa del ReyBarcelona
UEFA Champions LeagueBarcelona (2009, 2011 and more)
UEFA Super CupBarcelona
FIFA Club World CupBarcelona
World CupSpain, 2010 (South Africa)
European ChampionshipSpain, 2008 and 2012

The same years that produced Barcelona's treble-winning 2008-09 and 2014-15 sides also produced Spain's unmatched run of Euro 2008, World Cup 2010 and Euro 2012. That double window — club dominance and international dominance at the same moment — is what makes the generation so exceptional.

Messi: The Grand Slam Plus

Lionel Messi completed the same clean sweep and then added more. On top of the Barcelona and Spain-era trophies he won a tenth La Liga, the Copa America with Argentina in 2021 and 2024, and the World Cup in 2022, finally answering the one question that had followed him his whole career. He is the only player in this list to hold every major trophy simultaneously and an Olympic gold medal.

The Non-European Exception

The grand slam is not confined to Europe. Cafu, the Brazilian right-back, won two World Cups (1994 and 2002) with Brazil and the UEFA Champions League with AC Milan in 2007 — a rare South American who managed both club and international dominance. Brazilian legends like Ronaldo (two World Cups, La Liga, Serie A) and Ronaldinho (World Cup, Champions League) came close, but a complete collection is rarer than most fans assume.

The rarest number: Since 1966, only a handful of players have won a World Cup and a Champions League in the same career — and almost all of them came from the 2008-2015 Barcelona-Spain cycle.

Why So Few Ever Complete It

There is a simple arithmetic reason the grand slam is so rare. A player's club career peaks in his mid-20s, but a World Cup only arrives every four years, and a national team's window rarely matches a player's personal peak. Xavi and Iniesta got lucky twice: their prime coincided with Spain's greatest team, and Barcelona's greatest team.

The next player to win everything will need the same double stroke of fortune — and a decade of trophy-laden club dominance. It is why football's most decorated players are almost always found on the same teams, in the same eras.
